items.prose: A school garden is split into 20 equal beds. Potatoes fill $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of the garden and beans fill $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of it. The rest is for flowers.

feedback.correct: One quarter of 20 beds is $20 \div 4 = 5$ beds.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Split the 20 beds into 4 equal groups, then take 1 of the groups.

byKey.flipped: You worked out $20 \times 4$. A quarter of 20 is less than 20: $20 \div 4 = 5$.
byKey.three-quarters: 15 beds is the other three quarters. Beans fill one quarter: $20 \div 4 = 5$ beds.

explain.text: Cut the 20 beds into 4 equal groups of 5. One of those groups is beans. That is 5 beds.

parts.question: What fraction of the garden is potatoes and beans together? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Rename both fractions in twentieths, the size of one bed, then count.

byKey.tops-bottoms: You added the tops and the bottoms to get $\tfrac{3}{9}$. In twentieths it is $\tfrac{8}{20} + \tfrac{5}{20} = \tfrac{13}{20}$.
byKey.tops-kept: You changed the bottoms to 20 but kept the tops 2 and 1. Both tops change too: $\tfrac{8}{20} + \tfrac{5}{20}$.

explain.text: One bed is $\tfrac{1}{20}$ of the garden. Beans take 5 beds and potatoes take $20 \div 5 \times 2 = 8$ beds. Together that is $\tfrac{8}{20} + \tfrac{5}{20} = \tfrac{13}{20}$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{13}{20}$ for potatoes and beans, what fraction of the garden is left for flowers? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write the whole garden in twentieths and take away the beds already used.

byKey.carried: That is $1 - \tfrac{1}{3}$, from adding tops and bottoms in part 2. With $\tfrac{13}{20}$ used, $\tfrac{7}{20}$ is left.
byKey.beds: 7 is the number of flower beds. As a fraction of the 20-bed garden it is $\tfrac{7}{20}$.

explain.text: One whole garden is $\tfrac{20}{20}$. Taking away $\tfrac{13}{20}$ leaves $\tfrac{7}{20}$. That is the 7 beds still free.

parts.question: Half of the flower part is roses. Using $\tfrac{7}{20}$ for flowers, what fraction of the whole garden is roses? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take a half of the flower fraction: multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.

byKey.doubled: You doubled the flower part. Half of it is smaller: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{7}{20} = \tfrac{7}{40}$.
byKey.added-half: You added a half. A half of the flower part means $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{7}{20} = \tfrac{7}{40}$.
byKey.carried: That is half of $\tfrac{2}{3}$, the flower part from adding tops and bottoms. Half of $\tfrac{7}{20}$ is $\tfrac{7}{40}$.

explain.text: Roses are $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of $\tfrac{7}{20}$ of the garden. Multiply tops and bottoms: $\tfrac{1 \times 7}{2 \times 20} = \tfrac{7}{40}$. That is three and a half beds out of 20.

items.prose: A baker has $\tfrac{5}{6}$ kg of rye flour. Each rye loaf needs $\tfrac{1}{5}$ kg of flour.

parts.question: How many fifths of a kilogram fit into $\tfrac{5}{6}$ kg? Give an exact fraction or a mixed number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count how many fifths fit: divide by $\tfrac{1}{5}$, which is the same as multiplying by 5.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied, which gives a fifth of the flour. To count how many fifths fit, divide: $\tfrac{5}{6} \times 5 = \tfrac{25}{6}$.
byKey.wrong-flip: You flipped $\tfrac{5}{6}$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{5}$. Flip the fraction you divide by: $\tfrac{5}{6} \times \tfrac{5}{1}$.

explain.text: Dividing by $\tfrac{1}{5}$ counts fifths, and each whole holds 5 of them. So $\tfrac{5}{6} \div \tfrac{1}{5} = \tfrac{5}{6} \times 5 = \tfrac{25}{6}$. That is $4\tfrac{1}{6}$.

parts.question: Using $4\tfrac{1}{6}$ loaves' worth of flour, how many whole loaves can she bake?

feedback.correct: $4\tfrac{1}{6}$ is 4 wholes and a sixth more, so she can bake 4 whole loaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A loaf needs a whole fifth of a kilogram, so only the whole part counts.

byKey.rounded-up: One more loaf needs a full $\tfrac{1}{5}$ kg, but only a sixth of that is left. She bakes 4.
byKey.carried: That follows from a part 1 answer below 1, such as $\tfrac{1}{6}$. Using $4\tfrac{1}{6}$, she has enough for 4 whole loaves.

explain.text: $4\tfrac{1}{6}$ means 4 whole loaves' worth and $\tfrac{1}{6}$ of another. A sixth of a loaf's flour cannot make a loaf. She bakes 4.

parts.question: Using 4 loaves, how much flour is left over, in kg? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.correct: 4 loaves use $\tfrac{4}{5}$ kg. In thirtieths, $\tfrac{25}{30} - \tfrac{24}{30} = \tfrac{1}{30}$ kg.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the flour the 4 loaves use, then take it from $\tfrac{5}{6}$ kg in thirtieths.

byKey.one-loaf: You took away one loaf's $\tfrac{1}{5}$ kg. Four loaves use $\tfrac{4}{5}$ kg, which leaves $\tfrac{1}{30}$ kg.
byKey.tops-bottoms: You took tops from tops and bottoms from bottoms: $\tfrac{5 - 4}{6 - 5}$. Rename in thirtieths: $\tfrac{25}{30} - \tfrac{24}{30}$.
byKey.loaf-sixth: $\tfrac{1}{6}$ is the part of a loaf left over, not kilograms. A sixth of $\tfrac{1}{5}$ kg is $\tfrac{1}{30}$ kg.

explain.text: Four loaves use $4 \times \tfrac{1}{5} = \tfrac{4}{5}$ kg. In thirtieths that is $\tfrac{24}{30}$, and $\tfrac{5}{6} = \tfrac{25}{30}$. So $\tfrac{1}{30}$ kg is left.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{1}{30}$ kg left over, what fraction of her starting $\tfrac{5}{6}$ kg is that? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how many times $\tfrac{5}{6}$ fits into $\tfrac{1}{30}$: divide, by flipping and multiplying.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied $\tfrac{1}{30}$ by $\tfrac{5}{6}$. To compare with the start, divide: $\tfrac{1}{30} \times \tfrac{6}{5} = \tfrac{1}{25}$.
byKey.flipped: You worked out $\tfrac{5}{6} \div \tfrac{1}{30}$. The leftover is the small part, so divide it by the start.
byKey.carried: That is $\tfrac{19}{30} \div \tfrac{5}{6}$, from taking away one loaf. With $\tfrac{1}{30}$ kg left, the share is $\tfrac{1}{25}$.

explain.text: A fraction of the start means the leftover divided by the start. So $\tfrac{1}{30} \div \tfrac{5}{6} = \tfrac{1}{30} \times \tfrac{6}{5} = \tfrac{6}{150}$. That is $\tfrac{1}{25}$ of her flour.

items.prose: Two printers share one batch of leaflets. Printer A prints $\tfrac{3}{8}$ of the batch in an hour, and printer B prints $\tfrac{1}{3}$ of it in an hour. They start together.

parts.question: What fraction of the batch is printed in the first hour? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{9}{24}$ and $\tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{8}{24}$, so the first hour prints $\tfrac{9}{24} + \tfrac{8}{24} = \tfrac{17}{24}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rename both in twenty-fourths, a size both fit into, then count.

byKey.tops-bottoms: You added tops and bottoms to get $\tfrac{4}{11}$. That is less than A prints alone. Use twenty-fourths: $\tfrac{9}{24} + \tfrac{8}{24}$.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied the two fractions. Both printers add their work: $\tfrac{9}{24} + \tfrac{8}{24} = \tfrac{17}{24}$.

explain.text: Eighths and thirds both fit into twenty-fourths. Printer A does $\tfrac{9}{24}$ and printer B does $\tfrac{8}{24}$. Together that is $\tfrac{17}{24}$ of the batch.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{17}{24}$ printed, what fraction of the batch is still to print? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write the whole batch in twenty-fourths and take away what is printed.

byKey.carried: That is $1 - \tfrac{4}{11}$, from adding tops and bottoms in part 1. With $\tfrac{17}{24}$ printed, $\tfrac{7}{24}$ is left.
byKey.count: 7 is the count of twenty-fourths. As a fraction of the batch it is $\tfrac{7}{24}$.

explain.text: The whole batch is $\tfrac{24}{24}$. Taking away $\tfrac{17}{24}$ leaves $\tfrac{7}{24}$. That is a little under a third of the batch.

parts.question: Printer B then breaks down, and printer A finishes alone. Using $\tfrac{7}{24}$ of the batch left, how many hours does it take? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how many of A's hours, $\tfrac{3}{8}$ each, fit into $\tfrac{7}{24}$: divide.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied by $\tfrac{3}{8}$. To count how many hours fit, divide: $\tfrac{7}{24} \times \tfrac{8}{3} = \tfrac{7}{9}$.
byKey.flipped: You worked out $\tfrac{3}{8} \div \tfrac{7}{24}$. Divide the work left by A's work in an hour.
byKey.printer-b: You used printer B's rate, $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Printer A finishes, at $\tfrac{3}{8}$ an hour: $\tfrac{7}{24} \div \tfrac{3}{8}$.
byKey.minutes: That is the time in minutes. The question asks for hours: $\tfrac{7}{9}$ of an hour.

explain.text: Each hour printer A does $\tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{9}{24}$ of the batch. The $\tfrac{7}{24}$ left is 7 of those 9 pieces. So it takes $\tfrac{7}{24} \div \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{7}{9}$ of an hour.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{7}{9}$ of an hour for printer A alone, how many minutes does the whole batch take from the start? Give an exact fraction or a mixed number.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{7}{9}$ of 60 minutes is $\tfrac{420}{9} = 46\tfrac{2}{3}$. Add the first hour: $60 + 46\tfrac{2}{3} = 106\tfrac{2}{3}$ minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the part hour into minutes, then add the first hour.

byKey.rest-only: $46\tfrac{2}{3}$ minutes is printer A's time alone. Add the first 60 minutes: $106\tfrac{2}{3}$.
byKey.hundred: You used 100 minutes in an hour. An hour is 60 minutes: $60 + \tfrac{7}{9} \times 60 = 106\tfrac{2}{3}$.
byKey.carried-flipped: That uses $\tfrac{9}{7}$ of an hour from part 3. With $\tfrac{7}{9}$ of an hour, the total is $106\tfrac{2}{3}$ minutes.
byKey.hours: That is the whole time in hours, $1\tfrac{7}{9}$. In minutes it is $60 + 46\tfrac{2}{3} = 106\tfrac{2}{3}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{7}{9}$ of 60 minutes is $60 \div 9 \times 7 = 46\tfrac{2}{3}$ minutes. The two printers ran together for the first 60 minutes. So the batch takes $60 + 46\tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{320}{3}$ minutes.

items.prose: A café mixes squash in two jugs. Each jug is full and holds $\tfrac{3}{4}$ litre. In jug A, $\tfrac{4}{9}$ of the drink is cordial. In jug B, $\tfrac{5}{12}$ of the drink is cordial.

parts.question: Rename jug A's share, $\tfrac{4}{9}$, in thirty-sixths. How many thirty-sixths is it?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find what 9 is multiplied by to make 36, then multiply the top by the same number.

byKey.top-kept: You changed the bottom to 36 but kept the top. Both are multiplied by 4: $\tfrac{16}{36}$.
byKey.added: You added 27 to the top and the bottom. That changes the amount. Multiply both by 4 instead: $\tfrac{16}{36}$.
byKey.whole-fraction: That is the whole fraction, which still equals $\tfrac{4}{9}$. Type only the count of thirty-sixths: 16.

explain.text: Each ninth splits into 4 thirty-sixths, because $9 \times 4 = 36$. So 4 ninths become $4 \times 4 = 16$ thirty-sixths. The amount is the same, in smaller pieces.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{16}{36}$ for jug A, rename jug B's $\tfrac{5}{12}$ in thirty-sixths too. Which jug has the stronger mix?

options.why: The pieces differ in size: ninths are bigger than twelfths. In thirty-sixths, A has 16 and B has 15.
Both are under a half, but $\tfrac{16}{36}$ and $\tfrac{15}{36}$ differ by one thirty-sixth.

feedback.correct: Yes. With pieces of one size, 16 thirty-sixths beat 15.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two shares once both are in thirty-sixths.

byKey.b-top: A bigger top on smaller pieces need not be more. $\tfrac{4}{9} = \tfrac{16}{36}$ and $\tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{15}{36}$.
byKey.same: Close, but not equal: $\tfrac{16}{36}$ is one thirty-sixth more than $\tfrac{15}{36}$.

explain.text: Renamed in thirty-sixths, jug A is $\tfrac{16}{36}$ cordial and jug B is $\tfrac{15}{36}$. The pieces now match, so the counts decide. Jug A is a little stronger.

parts.question: How much cordial is in jug A, in litres? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take $\tfrac{4}{9}$ of the $\tfrac{3}{4}$ litre: multiply the tops and the bottoms.

byKey.added: You added the two fractions. A share of a jug is a fraction of a fraction: $\tfrac{4}{9} \times \tfrac{3}{4}$.
byKey.divided: You divided by $\tfrac{3}{4}$. Taking $\tfrac{4}{9}$ of the jug means multiplying: $\tfrac{12}{36} = \tfrac{1}{3}$.

explain.text: Jug A holds $\tfrac{3}{4}$ litre, and $\tfrac{4}{9}$ of that is cordial. Multiply: $\tfrac{4 \times 3}{9 \times 4} = \tfrac{12}{36}$. That is $\tfrac{1}{3}$ litre, less than either fraction.

parts.question: Jug B holds $\tfrac{5}{12} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{5}{16}$ litre of cordial. Using $\tfrac{1}{3}$ litre in jug A, how much cordial is in the two jugs together? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.correct: In forty-eighths, $\tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{16}{48}$ and $\tfrac{5}{16} = \tfrac{15}{48}$, so together $\tfrac{16}{48} + \tfrac{15}{48} = \tfrac{31}{48}$ litre.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Rename both in forty-eighths, a size thirds and sixteenths both fit into.

byKey.tops-bottoms: You added tops and bottoms to get $\tfrac{6}{19}$, less than jug A alone. Use forty-eighths: $\tfrac{16}{48} + \tfrac{15}{48}$.
byKey.carried: That uses $\tfrac{43}{36}$ for jug A, from adding in part 3. With $\tfrac{1}{3}$ litre, the total is $\tfrac{31}{48}$.

explain.text: Thirds and sixteenths both fit into forty-eighths. Jug A has $\tfrac{16}{48}$ litre and jug B has $\tfrac{15}{48}$ litre. Together that is $\tfrac{31}{48}$ litre of cordial.

parts.question: Both jugs are poured into one bowl, which then holds $\tfrac{3}{2}$ litres. Using $\tfrac{31}{48}$ litre of cordial, what fraction of the bowl is cordial? Give an exact fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the cordial by the whole bowl: flip $\tfrac{3}{2}$ and multiply.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied by $\tfrac{3}{2}$. A share of the bowl is the cordial divided by the bowl: $\tfrac{31}{48} \times \tfrac{2}{3}$.
byKey.shares-added: You added the two jugs' shares. The bowl holds two jugs, so the share is half of that: $\tfrac{31}{72}$.

explain.text: The share of the bowl is the cordial divided by the whole bowl. So $\tfrac{31}{48} \div \tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{31}{48} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{62}{144} = \tfrac{31}{72}$. It sits between the two jugs' shares, as a mix should.
